title: Conduit bending constants, marks and NEC rules
source: Written from the ELECT 275 conduit bending study guide.

cards.front: Which bender mark do you line up for a standard 90° stub-up?
cards.back: The arrow (front of the hook).

cards.front: Which bender mark is used for the back of a 90° (back-to-back 90s)?
cards.back: The star, at the back heel of the shoe.

cards.front: Which bender mark is used for the center bend of a 3-point saddle?
cards.back: The notch, rim or teardrop at the center of the bend.

cards.front: Which mark do you use for the two bends of an offset?
cards.back: The arrow, for both marks.

cards.front: Which marks do you use for the outer bends of a 3-point saddle?
cards.back: The arrow.

cards.front: How do you check bend angle with a hand bender?
cards.back: Read the degree scale cast on the side of the shoe, or check with a torpedo level or protractor.

cards.front: Which EMT shoe bends 1/2 in. rigid (RMC/IMC)?
cards.back: The 3/4 in. EMT shoe. The 1 in. EMT shoe bends 3/4 in. rigid.

cards.front: How do you find the mark for a 90° stub-up?
cards.back: Mark = desired stub height − bender deduction (take-up). Line the mark up with the arrow.

cards.front: 90° deduction for 1/2 in. EMT?
cards.back: 5 in.

cards.front: 90° deduction for 3/4 in. EMT?
cards.back: 6 in.

cards.front: 90° deduction for 1 in. EMT?
cards.back: 8 in.

cards.front: 90° deduction for 1-1/4 in. EMT?
cards.back: 11 in.

cards.front: 90° deductions for 1/2, 3/4 and 1 in. rigid (RMC)?
cards.back: 6 in., 8 in. and 11 in. Rigid uses the next-size-up EMT shoe, so it takes that shoe's deduction.

cards.front: What is gain?
cards.back: The length saved because a bend takes a curved shortcut. Total pipe needed = leg 1 + leg 2 − gain.

cards.front: Worked: 12 in. stub with 1/2 in. EMT. Where is the mark?
cards.back: 12 − 5 = 7 in. from the end, lined up with the arrow.

cards.front: Worked: 18 in. stub with 3/4 in. rigid. Where is the mark?
cards.back: 18 − 8 = 10 in. from the end, on the arrow.

cards.front: How do you make the second bend of a back-to-back 90?
cards.back: Measure the outside-to-outside distance from the back of the first 90, line that mark up with the star, hook facing away. No deduction.

cards.front: Why over-bend rigid conduit slightly?
cards.back: Steel RMC springs back. Over-bend about 2° to 3°.

cards.front: How far apart are the two marks of an offset?
cards.back: Offset height × the multiplier for the bend angle.

cards.front: Offset multiplier for 10° bends?
Offset multiplier for 22.5° bends?
Offset multiplier for 30° bends?
Offset multiplier for 45° bends?
cards.back: 1.4 (exactly 1.414)

cards.front: Offset multiplier for 60° bends?
cards.back: 1.2 (exactly 1.155)

cards.front: What is the multiplier mathematically?
cards.back: The cosecant of the bend angle: 1 ÷ sin(angle). For 30°, 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.

cards.front: Shrinkage per inch of offset height for 10°, 22.5°, 30°, 45° and 60° bends?
When bending toward an obstacle, what do you do with shrinkage?
cards.back: Add it to the distance to the obstacle when placing the first mark.

cards.front: Worked: 6 in. offset with 30° bends. Mark spacing and shrinkage?
cards.back: 6 × 2 = 12 in. between marks. Shrinkage 6 × 1/4 = 1-1/2 in.

cards.front: Worked: 4 in. offset with 45° bends. Mark spacing?
Why choose a smaller offset angle like 22.5° over 45°?
cards.back: Less shrinkage and easier wire pulling, but the offset takes more length.

cards.front: What are the bend angles of a 3-point saddle?
3-point saddle: where is the center mark?
cards.back: Distance to the center of the obstacle + 3/16 in. per inch of obstacle height. Line it up with the notch or rim.

cards.front: 3-point saddle: where are the outer marks?
cards.back: 2-1/2 in. per inch of obstacle height on each side of the center mark, lined up with the arrow.

cards.front: Worked: 3-point saddle over a 4 in. pipe, center 30 in. from the end. Marks?
cards.back: Center at 30 + 4 × 3/16 = 30-3/4 in. Outer marks 4 × 2-1/2 = 10 in. each side: 20-3/4 in. and 40-3/4 in.

cards.front: What is a 4-point saddle?
cards.back: Two offsets back to back, usually 30° or 22.5°, to go over a wide obstacle.

cards.front: 4-point saddle: list the four marks.
cards.back: 1: distance to obstacle + shrinkage. 2: mark 1 + height × multiplier. 3: mark 2 + obstacle width. 4: mark 3 + height × multiplier.

cards.front: What bends make a box offset?
cards.back: Two 10° bends, usually for a 3/8 or 1/2 in. offset into a box.

cards.front: Worked: 1/2 in. box offset. How far apart are the marks?
cards.back: 0.5 × 6.0 = 3 in. The first mark is 2 to 3 in. from the end.

cards.front: Box offset and a stub-up on the same piece: which bend first?
cards.back: The box offset first, then measure the stub from that end.

cards.front: Maximum total degrees of bends between pull points?
cards.back: 360°, counting offsets and saddles (NEC 358.26 EMT, 344.26 RMC).

cards.front: How many degrees does a 3-point saddle (22.5-45-22.5) add toward the 360° limit?
EMT securing and support distances?
cards.back: Within 3 ft of every box, cabinet or fitting, and at least every 10 ft (NEC 358.30(A)).

cards.front: RMC securing and support distances?
cards.back: Within 3 ft of every box or fitting and every 10 ft; longer spacing is allowed for straight runs with threaded couplings (NEC 344.30).

cards.front: Why does the NEC limit bends between pull points?
cards.back: Every bend adds pulling tension. Too many bends damage the conductor insulation during the pull.
